June 10, 2026 
 
The Honorable Mehmet Oz 
Administrator 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services 
Attention: CMS-0057-P 
7500 Security Boulevard 
Baltimore, MD 21244 
 
Re: 
Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; 
Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage 
Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children’s Health 
Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of 
Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges (CMS–0062–P) 
 
Dear Administrator Mehmet Oz: 
 
On behalf of the undersigned 17 organizations representing more than 207,000 osteopathic physicians 
(DOs) and medical students, thank you for this opportunity to comment on the 2026 CMS Interoperability 
Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule. We appreciate the work that the Centers for 
Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) has undertaken to address physician administrative burden and 
the agency’s commitment to pursing reforms that will improve care delivery and access. 
 
Osteopathic physicians are trained in a patient-centered, whole-person approach to care. We believe 
policies should be tailored to empower physicians in partnering with patients to make treatment decisions 
that will result in the best outcomes. The prior authorization (PA) process places substantial time and 
cost burdens on physician practices, and care delays associated with PA often lead to serious adverse 
events among patients. 
 
We commend CMS’ efforts to improve the PA process and extend the requirements from the 2024 
Promoting Interoperability and Improving Prior Authorization Processes final rule to cover PA for drugs. 
We commented on the 2024 rulemaking with a request for CMS to address the growing care barriers 
associated with drug PAs and appreciate CMS for its work to be responsive to  our organizations and 
other stakeholder feedback.  
 
This proposed rule makes critical changes that will streamline prior authorization by (1) establishing 
technical standards and requiring use of specific implementation guides that will drive broader electronic 
prior authorization for drugs, (2) ensure that patients and physicians have essential information about 
prior authorizations submitted, (3) improve communication between payors and physicians, and (4) 
create greater accountability in PA processes. Most notably, our organizations urge CMS to finalize 
proposals to require each impacted payor to implement and maintain standards-based application 
programming interfaces (APIs) that support critical functions associated with prior authorization. As 
physicians continue to face interoperability challenges, particularly around the ability to exchange 
information with health plans despite existing API requirements, we support the adoption of standards 
to ensure that data can be shared seamlessly, and PA can be performed for drugs and services within 
physicians’ EMR workflows. 
 
 
Provisions of this rule extend beyond adoption of electronic PA for drugs, and we appreciate CMS’ 
efforts improve the PA process overall. However, we offer the following recommendations to strengthen 
the agency’s proposals and ensure that they fulfill the intended goal of alleviating burden to the greatest 
extent possible: 
 
• Expanding Communication of Prior Authorization Denials for Drugs: While we urge CMS 
to finalize provisions requiring plans to provide physicians and patients with denial reasons for 
denied PA requests, we urge the agency to build upon these provisions by adopting policy that 
will help reduce inappropriate denials. CMS should require potential adverse decisions to be 
reviewed by relevant specialists for the drugs and service prior to issuing any denial and require 
that PA requirements for items and services be based upon publicly available evidence or clinical 
guidelines. CMS already requires that PA denials for items and services in Medicare Advantage 
be reviewed by relevant specialists, and we urge CMS to expand upon this effort.  
 
• Prior Authorization Metrics: While we strongly support CMS’ proposal to require that 
impacted payors annually report PA metrics, we believe that the required metrics are not adequate 
to provide sufficient transparency and build trust with patients. CMS’ proposal would require 
reporting of aggregate data points on approval rates, denial rates, average time elapsed to 
decisions, and other measures regarding prior authorizations at the issuer or contract level. 
However, this reporting will have limited utility to beneficiaries shopping for plans, or providers 
contracting with payers, due to its lack of specificity. Requiring reporting based on specialty, 
therapeutic area, drug, or individual service will provide more meaningful information to patients 
and providers around how plans perform on various prior authorization metrics. Such data would 
also help identify specific services where PA may be inappropriate.  
 
• Timeframes for Prior Authorization Decisions: For most drug prior authorizations across 
impacted payors, CMS proposes that payors make PA determinations no later than 24 hours after 
receiving an urgent request and 72 hours for standard requests. For items and services, CMS’ will 
maintain its requirement of 7 days for standard requests and 72 hours for expedited requests. 
There are also separate timeframes proposed for drugs that are not covered outpatient drugs. In 
general, we appreciate the 24-hour time frame for drugs, but  request the proposed timeframes of 
nondrug requests be shortened to 72 hours for standard requests and 24 hours for urgent requests. 
Timeframes should be reduced to the greatest extent possible to minimize unnecessary care 
delays. This will ensure patients can receive timely care when they need it. Additionally, we urge 
CMS to consider establishing requirements that plans be capable of issuing real-time decisions 
for PA requests. 
 
While this rule makes important strides in streamlining the prior authorization process and promoting 
transparency for drugs, we urge CMS to continue building on these efforts and pursue comprehensive 
PA reform. Prior authorization burden can be further alleviated by: 
 
1. Limiting the application of PA and step therapy to drugs and services that are truly of concern 
for patient safety, and preventing low-value PA policies that create burden and provide limited 
benefit to patient safety or appropriate utilization; 
 
2. Ensuring that any PA policies are developed by experts in the relevant specialty using publicly 
available evidence-based criteria, and that adverse decisions or peer-reviews are conducted by 
relevant specialists; and 
 
3. Ensuring physicians with strong records of proper documentation and approval for PAs are 
granted relief from requirements through carefully designed gold card programs.   
 
Our organizations greatly appreciate the effort and focus CMS has placed on improving PA and 
addressing burden across its recent rulemaking efforts. We look forward to continuing to work with CMS 
to improve timely access to care, to allow physicians to spend more time with patients, and to adopt PA 
reforms across insurance markets. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
American Osteopathic Association 
American Academy of Osteopathy 
American College of Osteopathic Emergency Physicians 
American College of Osteopathic Internists 
American College of Osteopathic Family Physicians 
American College of Osteopathic Neurologists and Psychiatrists 
American College of Osteopathic Obstetricians and Gynecologists 
American College of Osteopathic Pediatricians 
American College of Osteopathic Surgeons 
American Osteopathic Academy of Orthopedics 
American Osteopathic Academy of Sports Medicine 
American Osteopathic College of Anesthesiologists 
American Osteopathic College of Occupational and Preventive Medicine

American Osteopathic College of Pathologists

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** American Osteopathic Association and 16 allied osteopathic specialty organizations.
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association; Healthcare Provider.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Represents more than 207,000 osteopathic physicians and medical students. The comment describes osteopathic physicians' patient-centered, whole-person approach to care and physician experience with prior authorization burden.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The osteopathic physician organizations strongly support CMS proposals to extend electronic prior authorization reforms to drugs and require standards-based APIs and implementation guides. They recommend strengthening the rule with more robust denial safeguards, more granular prior authorization metrics, shorter decision timeframes, real-time decision capability, limits on low-value prior authorization and step therapy, evidence-based criteria, specialist review, and gold card relief.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** No specific CFR citations are cited. The letter references CMS-0062-P and the 2024 Promoting Interoperability and Improving Prior Authorization Processes final rule.
- **Standards referenced:** Standards-based APIs; implementation guides; electronic prior authorization; EMR workflows. The comment does not name specific FHIR IGs or NCPDP standards.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** The organizations state that prior authorization creates substantial practice costs and treatment delays, and they support extending the 2024 prior authorization reforms to drugs. They view required technical standards and implementation guides as necessary to make PA workable in physician EMR workflows.
- **Specific request:** Finalize requirements for impacted payers to implement and maintain standards-based APIs supporting prior authorization functions for drugs and services.

**Topic 2: Prior Authorization Denial Safeguards**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** The commenters support requiring plans to provide denial reasons but argue that transparency alone will not prevent inappropriate denials.
- **Specific request:** Require potential adverse decisions to be reviewed by relevant specialists before denial, and require PA criteria for items and services to be based on publicly available evidence or clinical guidelines.

**Topic 3: Prior Authorization Metrics and Transparency**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Aggregate approval, denial, and decision-time metrics at the issuer or contract level are not specific enough to help patients compare plans or help providers assess payer performance.
- **Specific request:** Require reporting by specialty, therapeutic area, drug, or individual service so beneficiaries and providers can identify patterns and potentially inappropriate PA use.

**Topic 4: Decision Timeframes and Real-Time Capability**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** The commenters appreciate the proposed 24-hour urgent timeframe for drugs, but contend that shorter timeframes are needed to minimize unnecessary delays in care.
- **Specific request:** Shorten non-drug PA decision timeframes to 72 hours for standard requests and 24 hours for urgent requests, and consider requiring plans to be capable of issuing real-time PA decisions.

**Topic 5: Comprehensive Prior Authorization Reform**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** The organizations argue that drug PA interoperability improvements are important but insufficient to address broader PA burden.
- **Specific request:** Limit PA and step therapy to drugs and services truly raising patient safety concerns; require expert-developed, evidence-based PA policies; require relevant specialist peer review; and create carefully designed gold card programs for physicians with strong approval and documentation histories.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S1:** The comment supports making standards and implementation guides mandatory rather than merely recommended, because required standards are viewed as necessary for seamless data exchange and EMR-integrated PA.
- **S12:** The comment identifies physician workflow and payer-provider interoperability challenges as central implementation issues for drug PA APIs.
- **S16:** The comment supports requiring specific denial reasons, but recommends adding specialist review and evidence-based criteria to reduce inappropriate denials.
- **S18:** The comment supports mandatory implementation guide requirements and frames them as a way to reduce provider burden rather than as an undue burden.
- **S20:** The comment supports 24-hour urgent drug PA decision timeframes and asks CMS to reduce timeframes as much as possible.
- **S43:** The comment asks CMS to shorten non-drug PA timeframes to 72 hours for standard requests and 24 hours for urgent requests, aligning broader PA processes with more timely drug PA expectations.
- **S66-S82:** The comment generally addresses broader PA reforms such as step therapy limits, evidence-based criteria, and gold carding, but does not map those recommendations to a specific numbered RFI.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize standards-based API requirements for impacted payers to support electronic PA for drugs and services.
2. Finalize requirements to provide denial reasons for denied drug PA requests.
3. Require relevant specialist review before adverse PA decisions are issued.
4. Require PA criteria to be based on publicly available evidence or clinical guidelines.
5. Require more granular PA metrics by specialty, therapeutic area, drug, or individual service.
6. Shorten non-drug PA timeframes to 72 hours for standard requests and 24 hours for urgent requests.
7. Consider requiring plans to support real-time PA decisions.
8. Limit PA and step therapy to drugs and services with genuine patient safety concerns.
9. Adopt gold card programs for physicians with strong records of PA approval and documentation.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Administrative burden on physician practices; care delays; inappropriate denials; insufficient specificity in PA metrics; low-value PA and step therapy policies.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Serious adverse events from PA-related delays, limited usefulness of aggregate metrics to patients and providers, and continued burden if PA reforms are not comprehensive.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Persistent payer-provider interoperability challenges and the need to integrate PA processes into physicians' EMR workflows.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** The signatories represent more than 207,000 osteopathic physicians and medical students.
- **Studies or research referenced:** No external studies are cited.
- **Examples provided:** The comment cites Medicare Advantage policy requiring relevant specialist review for PA denials as a model CMS should expand.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Physicians, patients, impacted payers, beneficiaries shopping for plans, providers contracting with payers, and plans administering PA.
- **Economic implications:** The comment emphasizes substantial time and cost burdens on physician practices but does not quantify implementation costs.
- **Technical feasibility:** The commenters believe standards-based APIs and required implementation guides are feasible and necessary, while noting ongoing interoperability challenges.
- **Patient care impact:** The comment argues that faster, more transparent, and clinically grounded PA processes would reduce treatment delays and improve timely access to care.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive
- **Tone:** Professional; Collaborative; Provider-focused
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "The prior authorization (PA) process places substantial time and cost burdens on physician practices, and care delays associated with PA often lead to serious adverse events among patients." - Context: Opening statement explaining why physician organizations support CMS prior authorization reform.
2. "Most notably, our organizations urge CMS to finalize proposals to require each impacted payor to implement and maintain standards-based application programming interfaces (APIs) that support critical functions associated with prior authorization." - Context: Core support for the proposed standards-based PA API requirements.
3. "CMS should require potential adverse decisions to be reviewed by relevant specialists for the drugs and service prior to issuing any denial and require that PA requirements for items and services be based upon publicly available evidence or clinical guidelines." - Context: Recommendation to strengthen denial protections.
4. "Requiring reporting based on specialty, therapeutic area, drug, or individual service will provide more meaningful information to patients and providers around how plans perform on various prior authorization metrics." - Context: Argument for more granular PA transparency metrics.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - The comment addresses PA decision timeframes and asks CMS to shorten non-drug PA deadlines while preserving rapid drug determinations.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - The comment emphasizes substantial time and cost burdens on physician practices from PA, though it does not quantify costs.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Reducing physician administrative burden is a central theme, including EMR workflow integration and limiting low-value PA.
- [ ] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - Not addressed.
- [ ] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - Not addressed.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - The comment supports standards-based APIs as a practical way to improve payer-provider data exchange and PA workflows.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - The commenters support required implementation guides and standards, though they do not discuss maturity concerns.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - The comment repeatedly links PA reform to avoiding treatment delays and improving timely access to care.
- [ ] **REGULATORY-AUTHORITY** - Not addressed.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - The comment focuses on coordination between payers and physicians through interoperable PA workflows.
- [ ] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - Not addressed.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - The comment supports denial reasons and more granular PA metrics for patients and providers.
- [ ] **SMALL-PAYER-IMPACT** - Not addressed.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - The comment stresses that PA should occur within physicians' EMR workflows.
- [ ] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Not addressed.
